a: Ramathaim-zophim
p: Samuel's home town is called Ramathaim here and Ramah everywhere else. Its location is debated.
b: Ramathaim means "the two heights," and the story soon shortens it to Ramah, "the height" (1:19; 2:11; 7:17). "Zophim" may come from Zuph, the ancestor named at the end of the verse and the region of 9:5. Many scholars think the Hebrew first read "from Ramathaim, a Zuphite" (see the variant). Most place the town in the hills of Ephraim north-west of Jerusalem; one common candidate is Rentis, and another is er-Ram, the Ramah of Benjamin. Early Christian writers such as Eusebius linked Ramathaim with Arimathea, the home of Joseph who buried Jesus (Matthew 27:57).

a: an Ephrathite
p: The Hebrew word can mean someone from Ephraim or someone from Ephrathah. Chronicles makes Elkanah a Levite.
b: Ephrati means an Ephraimite in Judges 12:5 and someone from Ephrathah, that is Bethlehem, in Ruth 1:2. Here, with "the hill country of Ephraim," most read it as "Ephraimite" in the sense of where the family lived. 1 Chronicles 6:22–28 and 6:33–38 list Elkanah and Samuel among the descendants of Kohath, son of Levi. Traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, combine the two: a Levite family living in Ephraim, as Levites did (Joshua 21:5, 20). Many critical scholars think the Chronicler gave Samuel a Levite family tree because he serves at the sanctuary and offers sacrifices (7:9).
r: Judges 12:5; Ruth 1:2; 1 Chronicles 6:22–28; 1 Chronicles 6:33–38; Joshua 21:5; Joshua 21:20; 7:9

a: He had two wives
p: A husband, a loved but barren wife and a rival with children: the setup of Sarah and Hagar, and Rachel and Leah.
b: The Bible's stories of two wives are rarely happy. Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16), Rachel and Leah (Genesis 29–30): each time the loved wife is barren and the other has children and uses them as a weapon. Readers who know Genesis would expect Hannah, like Rachel, to receive a son of destiny. The law of Moses tolerated more than one wife but tried to protect the unloved one (Deuteronomy 21:15–17). Many readers assume Elkanah took a second wife because Hannah had no children, but the text does not say so.

a: the LORD of Armies
p: This is the first time in the Bible that God is called YHWH tseva'ot, "the LORD of Armies."
b: "The LORD" in capitals stands for God's personal name, YHWH, which Jews read aloud as Adonai, "my Lord" (see the book introduction). Here it is joined to tseva'ot, "armies" or "hosts," a title that appears first in this verse and more than 250 times later, mostly in the prophets. The armies may be Israel's troops (17:45), the stars (Isaiah 40:26) or the angels of God's court (1 Kings 22:19). The title is tied to the ark at Shiloh (4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2). The Greek keeps the Hebrew as Sabaoth (Romans 9:29; James 5:4), and older English has "the LORD of hosts."
r: 4:4; 17:45; 2 Samuel 6:2; Isaiah 6:3; Isaiah 40:26; 1 Kings 22:19; Romans 9:29; James 5:4

a: Shiloh
p: Shiloh, in the hills of Ephraim, held the ark and Israel's chief sanctuary until the Philistine wars.
b: Joshua set up the tent of meeting at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1), and Judges 21:19 places the town between Bethel and Shechem, at modern Khirbet Seilun. Danish digs in the 1920s and 1930s and Israel Finkelstein's dig of 1981–1984 found a large hilltop village of the Iron Age I (about 1150–1050 BC) with storerooms full of jars, destroyed by fire in the eleventh century BC. Many link that fire to the Philistine victory of chapter 4. Psalm 78:60 and Jeremiah 7:12–14 remember Shiloh as the place God abandoned, though the book of Samuel never says that the town was destroyed.

a: Hophni and Phinehas
p: Both of Eli's sons have names that most scholars trace to Egyptian.
b: Phinehas is generally taken to be the Egyptian Pa-nehasy, "the Nubian" or "the dark-skinned one," a name also borne by Aaron's zealous grandson (Numbers 25:7–13). Hophni is often explained from an Egyptian word for "tadpole," though that is less certain. Egyptian names in the priestly line fit the memory of Israel's priests coming out of Egypt (2:27). The reader who knows Numbers 25 hears the irony: the first Phinehas was praised for defending God's honor, while this one despises the LORD's offering (2:17).

a: Her rival
p: The Hebrew word for a second wife is "rival." It says what such marriages were often like.
b: Tsarah means "rival" or "one who distresses," from the root for being hemmed in. Later Hebrew uses it as the ordinary word for a co-wife, and Leviticus 18:18 uses the verb when it forbids marrying a woman's sister "as a rival." The verse also says Peninnah taunted Hannah "to stir her up," literally "to make her thunder," a rare form of the verb used for God's thunder in 2:10 and 7:10. The book may be hinting that the LORD will answer this thunder with his own. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and the Greek reads it differently.

a: worth more to you than ten sons
p: Elkanah's words use the same Hebrew form as the women's praise of Ruth: "worth more to you than seven sons."
b: The townswomen tell Naomi that Ruth "is worth more to you than seven sons" (Ruth 4:15), and the Hebrew construction is the same. There it is true praise; here it is a husband's well-meant but clumsy comfort. Elkanah loves Hannah (1:5), but his questions put his own feelings at the center. Many readers, such as Robert Alter, hear the gap between his love and her grief, and note that Hannah never answers him. She takes her sorrow to the LORD instead (1:10).

a: the LORD's temple
p: Samuel calls the Shiloh shrine a "temple" with doorposts and doors, though elsewhere it is a tent.
b: Hekhal, "palace" or "temple," is the word later used for Solomon's temple. Shiloh's shrine has a doorpost here, doors in 3:15 and a place to sleep in 3:3. Yet 2:22 and Psalm 78:60 speak of a tent. Traditional readers have combined the two: the Mishnah says the Shiloh sanctuary had stone walls below and tent curtains above (Mishnah Zevachim 14:6). Many critical scholars think the Shiloh shrine was a real building and that the tent belongs to the Priestly writers' picture of Israel's early worship. Archaeologists have not found the building.

a: Bitter in her soul
p: The phrase is used of people at the end of their strength: Naomi, Job, and David's men at Ziklag.
b: Marat nefesh, "bitter of soul," is the Hebrew Bible's phrase for deep inner pain. Naomi says the Almighty has made her life very bitter (Ruth 1:20); Job speaks "in my soul's bitterness" (Job 7:11); David's men are "bitter in soul" when their families are taken (30:6). Hannah's bitterness becomes prayer, not complaint against others. Jewish readers have long taken her as the model of a person who brings grief straight to God.

a: She made a vow
p: Under the law of Numbers 30, a husband could cancel his wife's vow. Elkanah lets Hannah's stand.
b: Numbers 30:6–8 says that if a married woman makes a vow and her husband keeps quiet on the day he hears of it, the vow holds; if he forbids it, it is canceled. Hannah makes her vow without asking Elkanah, and in 1:23 he confirms it. Her vow also gives away what she most wants: a son, given back to God. Readers often compare Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:30–31), made rashly by a man, with this one, made with care by a woman.

a: No razor will ever go up on his head
p: No razor on the head is the mark of a Nazirite (Numbers 6:5) and of Samson (Judges 13:5).
b: The same Hebrew phrase is said of Samson, "God's Nazirite from the womb" (Judges 13:5), and the Nazirite law says "no razor is to touch his head" (Numbers 6:5). The Masoretic Text never calls Samuel a Nazirite, but the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a does at 1:22, and the Greek adds here that he will drink no wine (see the variants). The rabbis debated it: Rabbi Nehorai said Samuel was a Nazirite, while Rabbi Yose read the word morah as "fear" of man rather than "razor" (Mishnah Nazir 9:5). Sirach 46:13 calls him "a Nazirite of the LORD" in its Hebrew text.

a: a male child
p: Hannah asks for "seed of men," a rare phrase. It means a boy, and perhaps a real man of worth.
b: The Hebrew zera' anashim appears only here. Most take it simply as "a male child." The rabbis played with it: the Talmud offers readings such as a son equal to two great men, Moses and Aaron, or a son who is neither too tall nor too short, neither too wise nor too foolish, but ordinary (Bavli Berakhot 31b). Some modern readers see a quiet contrast with Saul, who is chosen for his looks (9:2).

a: Hannah was speaking silently
p: Silent prayer was unusual enough that Eli thought she was drunk. The rabbis learned how to pray from her.
b: In the ancient world prayers and even reading were normally said aloud. Hannah prays "in her heart" with moving lips and no sound. The Talmud draws rules from the verse for the main Jewish prayer, the Amidah: pray with the heart's attention, form the words with the lips, and do not raise the voice (Bavli Berakhot 31a). Christian writers have seen her as a model of inward prayer. The literary point is sharp as well: Israel's priest cannot tell a praying woman from a drunk one, while his own sons go unchecked (2:12–17).

a: I have poured my soul out before the LORD
p: Hannah's words became the Bible's picture of honest prayer in the psalms.
b: The image of pouring out the soul or heart before God returns in the psalms: "pouring out my soul within me" (Psalm 42:4) and "pour out your hearts in front of him" (Psalm 62:8), and in Lamentations 2:19, "Empty your heart like water." Hannah answers Eli's charge about drink with an image of liquid: she has not poured wine into herself, she has poured herself out. Samuel's Mizpah ceremony of pouring water before the LORD may echo it (7:6).

a: a worthless woman
p: Hannah refuses the label "daughter of beliyya'al." The same label fits Eli's own sons (2:12).
b: The Hebrew is bat beliyya'al, "a daughter of worthlessness." Beliyya'al probably means "no-worth" or "no-rising," and "sons of beliyya'al" are lawless men (Deuteronomy 13:13; Judges 19:22). The book uses the phrase as a thread: Hannah is wrongly suspected of it, Eli's sons truly are "sons of beliyya'al" (2:12), and the men who despise Saul are too (10:27). In later Jewish writings Belial became a name for the devil, as in the Dead Sea Scrolls and in Paul's question "what agreement does Christ have with Belial?" (2 Corinthians 6:15).

a: May the God of Israel give you what you asked him for
p: The Hebrew verb can be read as a wish ("may he give") or as a prediction ("he will give").
b: Yitten can be a simple future or a wish. Most translations take it as a priestly blessing. Either way, the verse sets up the key word of the whole story: sha'al, "ask," here twice in "your request that you asked." The root comes back in 1:20, 1:27 and 1:28, and again in 2:20. It is also the root of Saul's name, Sha'ul, "asked for" (see 1:28).
orig: יִתֵּן אֶת־שֵׁלָתֵךְ אֲשֶׁר שָׁאַלְתְּ (yitten et-shelatekh asher sha'alt)

a: the LORD remembered her
p: "Remembered" in the Bible means acting on a promise or a need, as with Noah, Rachel and Israel in Egypt.
b: When God "remembers" he acts: he remembered Noah and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1); "God remembered Rachel; God paid heed to her and opened her womb" (Genesis 30:22); he remembered his covenant and rescued Israel from Egypt (Exodus 2:24). Hannah had asked God to "remember me" (1:11), and he does. The narrator puts the human act (Elkanah slept with Hannah) and God's act side by side, without making one cancel the other.

a: She named him Samuel
p: Hannah explains the name Samuel with the verb "ask," which fits the name Saul better. Scholars have long noticed this.
b: Shemu'el most likely means "name of God" or "his name is God." Hannah's reason, "I asked (sha'alti) the LORD for him," plays on sound, not strict meaning. The verb sha'al is the root of Sha'ul, Saul. Some critical scholars, in a line going back to the early twentieth century and discussed at length by Kyle McCarter, think this birth story was first told of Saul and later moved to Samuel. Most traditional readers, and many literary ones, take it as a deliberate play: Samuel, the one "asked" from God, will give Israel the king it "asked" for (8:10; 12:13). Radak explained the name as a short form of "asked from God."

a: he will appear in the LORD's presence
p: The Hebrew letters can say "see the face of the LORD." Scribes seem to have vowelled them to say "be seen."
b: The phrase nir'ah et-pene YHWH, "appear before the LORD," is the regular wording for the pilgrim feasts (Exodus 23:17; Deuteronomy 16:16). Many scholars, beginning in the nineteenth century, have argued that the consonants first meant "see the face of the LORD," and that the vowels were set to the passive so that no one would seem to claim to see God (Exodus 33:20). The point here is that Samuel will live his whole life in God's presence, as a servant of the sanctuary.

a: The boy was just a little boy
p: Children were weaned late in the ancient world, often at two or three. Samuel was still very young.
b: The odd Hebrew, "and the boy was a boy," stresses how young he was. A mother in 2 Maccabees reminds her son that she nursed him for three years (2 Maccabees 7:27), and Egyptian and Babylonian texts speak of nursing for up to three years. So Samuel was perhaps three when he came to Shiloh. Abraham held a feast when Isaac was weaned (Genesis 21:8). Hannah's gift of a three-year-old bull matches her three-year-old son. The Greek text is longer here (see the variants).

a: handed him over to the LORD
p: In 1:27–28 the root sha'al, "ask," appears four times. The last form, sha'ul, is the name Saul.
b: Hannah says: "This boy is what I prayed for, and the LORD has given me my request (she'elati) which I asked (sha'alti). So I in turn have made him asked-for (hish'iltihu) to the LORD. All his life he is sha'ul to the LORD." The causative form means to grant, lend or give over what was asked. Sha'ul is exactly the name Saul. No English word can carry this; the Plain uses "handed over." The story of the boy who is "asked" leads to the people who "ask" for a king (8:10) and to the king named "Asked" (9:2).

a: look at the misery of your servant
p: Mary's song uses the same Greek words as Hannah's prayer: God has looked on the lowliness of his servant.
b: In the Greek of 1:11 Hannah prays that God will "look upon the lowliness of your servant" (epiblepsēs epi tēn tapeinōsin tēs doulēs sou). Mary sings that God "has looked with care on the lowliness of his slave" (Luke 1:48), and Luke's Greek has the same verb, the same noun and the same word for "servant" (doulē, which the Plain of Luke renders "slave"). It is the closest verbal link between the two women, and it shows Luke reading Mary's story through Hannah's. The Hebrew 'oni means misery or affliction, the word used of Israel in Egypt (Exodus 3:7).

a: Hannah prayed
p: The song is called a prayer and put in Hannah's mouth, but it ends with a king. Readers explain this in several ways.
b: Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take the song as Hannah's own, spoken by the Spirit of prophecy: the Targum calls it a prophecy and expands it into a survey of Israel's history down to the end of days. Many critical scholars think it was an older psalm of victory, perhaps sung for a king (2:10), which the editor placed here because its line about the barren woman (2:5) fit Hannah. Literary readers note that, wherever it came from, it now frames the books of Samuel with David's song near the end (2 Samuel 22): both praise the God who brings down the proud and raises the low, and both end with "his anointed."

a: My heart leaps for joy in the LORD
p: Mary's song in Luke 1:46–55 follows Hannah's song closely, line after line.
b: Mary's song, the Magnificat, opens: "My soul declares how great the Lord is, and my spirit has found its gladness in God my Savior" (Luke 1:46–47), and goes on: "He has pulled rulers down from thrones and raised the lowly high. The hungry he has loaded with good things; the rich he has sent off with empty hands" (Luke 1:52–53). Both women sing about a child God has given, both praise God's holiness (2:2; Luke 1:49), and both turn one woman's joy into a song about God turning the world upside down. Christian readers since the early church have read the two songs together. Zechariah's song in the same chapter picks up Hannah's "horn" (Luke 1:69).

a: my horn is raised high
p: A horn stands for strength and honor, like the horns of a wild ox lifted in triumph.
b: In Hebrew poetry a raised horn pictures a strong animal holding its head high: victory, dignity, restored honor (Psalm 92:10; Psalm 75:10). A horn brought low or cut off is defeat (Lamentations 2:3). The song begins with Hannah's horn raised and ends with the horn of the LORD's anointed raised (2:10), so the image frames the whole poem. Luke's "horn of salvation" for the house of David (Luke 1:69) picks it up.

a: There is no rock like our God
p: Calling God a rock means he is a safe, solid place to stand and hide.
b: "Rock" is a common name for God in Hebrew poetry: in the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:4, 32:15, 32:31), in David's song (2 Samuel 22:2–3, 32, 47), and often in the Psalms (Psalm 18:31). In rocky Canaan, a crag was a refuge from enemies and a place where water might flow. The verse also states Israel's faith in one God plainly: "there is none but you," a thought close to Deuteronomy 32:39 and Isaiah 45:5.
r: Deuteronomy 32:4; Deuteronomy 32:31; 2 Samuel 22:32; Psalm 18:31; Isaiah 44:8; Isaiah 45:5

a: The childless woman bears seven
p: Seven is the number of fullness. Hannah, in fact, had six children in all (2:21).
b: Seven means a complete blessing, as in Ruth 4:15. Hannah later bears three more sons and two daughters (2:21), six children in all, so the number is poetry, not a count. Jeremiah turns the line around: "she who bore seven grows faint" (Jeremiah 15:9). Rashi records a midrash that as Hannah bore each child, Peninnah lost two. Many critical readers see the line as the reason this psalm was placed in Hannah's mouth.

a: he takes down to Sheol, and he brings up
p: Sheol is the world of the dead. Does the line mean rescue from near death, or the resurrection?
b: Sheol is the shadowy place of the dead in the Hebrew Bible (see the topic). To be "brought up from Sheol" usually means to be saved from deadly danger (Psalm 30:3; Jonah 2:6). The line echoes the Song of Moses: "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). The rabbis read that verse as a promise of the resurrection of the dead (Bavli Sanhedrin 91b), and Jewish prayer praises God who "makes the dead alive." Christian readers have heard Easter in it. Many modern scholars take it as poetry about God's power over life and death, without a teaching about resurrection yet.

a: he raises the needy from the garbage heap
t: From the dump to the throne
p: Psalm 113:7–8 repeats this line almost word for word.
b: The ashpot was the town's refuse heap, where the outcast and the sick sat and begged (compare Job 2:8; Lamentations 4:5). Psalm 113 uses nearly the same words: "He lifts the poor up out of the dust; he raises the needy from the garbage heap to give them a seat among nobles" (Psalm 113:7–8), and then: "The barren woman of the house he seats as a glad mother of children" (Psalm 113:9). The overlap with Hannah is striking. Whichever is older, both show that Israel sang this hope often. David, the shepherd raised to the throne, will live it out (2 Samuel 7:8).

a: The earth's pillars belong to the LORD
p: Hebrew poets pictured the earth resting on pillars. The point is that God holds up the world.
b: Several poems speak of the earth's pillars or foundations: Job 9:6, Psalm 75:3, Psalm 104:5. This was the common picture of the world in the ancient Near East, and the Bible's poets used it freely. The point of the line is not geography but power: the one who lifts the poor is the one who holds up the world, so no one can stop him. The Greek text lacks this line and has a different one in 2:9 (see the variant there).

a: his loyal ones
p: The word is chasid, from hesed, "loyal love": people who keep faith with God.
b: Chasidim are people marked by hesed, the loyal love that keeps a covenant. The Plain uses "loyal ones" so that the link with "loyal love" stays visible. In the Psalms the word often means God's faithful people (Psalm 30:4; Psalm 37:28). Later it named the pious party of the Maccabean age (1 Maccabees 2:42) and, much later, the Hasidic movement. The written Hebrew here has the singular, "his loyal one," and the reading tradition has the plural.

a: his anointed one's horn
p: The first time the Bible calls a king "his anointed," in Hebrew mashiach, the word that became "Messiah."
b: Mashiach means "anointed (with oil)." Priests were anointed (Leviticus 4:3), but here, beside "his king," it means a king. Israel has no king yet, so the line looks forward. Many critical scholars take it as a sign that the song was a royal psalm; traditional readers see prophecy. The Targum reads it of the King Messiah, and the rabbis and church fathers alike read it of the coming son of David. In the Greek it is christos, and Augustine took Hannah's song as a prophecy of Christ and the church (City of God 17.4). In 1 Samuel itself the title soon belongs to Saul (12:3; 24:6) and then David (16:6).

a: worthless men who did not know the LORD
t: Priests who did not know the LORD
p: Eli's sons are "sons of beliyya'al" (see 1:16), like the men of Gibeah in Judges 19:22.
b: Judges ends with a generation that did not know the LORD (Judges 2:10) and with "sons of beliyya'al" at Gibeah (Judges 19:22). Samuel opens with the same words used of the priests at Israel's chief shrine. "Know" in Hebrew is more than awareness: it is a relationship of loyalty, as when God says of Abraham, "I have known him" (Genesis 18:19). Samuel too "had not come to know the LORD yet" (3:7), but in his case it is a matter of time, not refusal.

a: This was how the priests dealt with the people
p: The law gave priests set portions of a sacrifice. Eli's sons took what they liked, and before God had his part.
b: Mishpat hakkohanim can mean "the priests' custom" or "the priests' rightful due." The law of Moses names the priest's share of a peace offering: the breast and the right thigh (Leviticus 7:34), or in Deuteronomy, "the foreleg, the two cheeks and the stomach" (Deuteronomy 18:3). Some scholars think the fork in the pot was an old Shiloh custom, a kind of lucky dip, and that the sin lies in 2:15–16. Others read the whole practice as greed. The Hebrew accents attach "the priests' custom with the people" to 2:13, as the Plain does; some versions join it to 2:12, "they did not know the LORD or the priests' due."

a: before the fat was even turned to smoke
p: In every peace offering the fat was burned on the altar first, as God's portion. Eli's sons took meat before that.
b: Leviticus says: "All the fat belongs to the LORD" (Leviticus 3:16), and the fat had to be turned to smoke on the altar before anyone ate (Leviticus 7:30–31). By demanding raw meat first, the priests put themselves ahead of God. The worshiper in 2:16 knows the law better than the priest. Raw meat could also be roasted, which many preferred to the boiled meat of sacrifice meals.

a: the men despised the LORD's offering
p: The sin was not only theft but contempt: they made the LORD's gift look cheap. Malachi says the same of later priests.
b: The verb ni'ets, "treat with contempt," is a strong word, used of those who despise God himself (Numbers 14:11, 23). The text seems to say that people also came to despise the offering because of the priests, and some readers take it that way. Malachi accuses the priests of his own day of the same thing (Malachi 1:6–14).

a: a linen ephod
t: A boy in a linen ephod
p: This simple linen ephod is not the high priest's gold ephod, but a garment worn by those who served at the shrine.
b: The word ephod covers more than one thing. The high priest's ephod was a richly woven vest with the breastpiece (Exodus 28:6). A plain "linen ephod" was worn by ordinary priests (22:18) and by David when he danced before the ark (2 Samuel 6:14). Elsewhere an ephod can be an object used to ask God questions (23:9; Judges 8:27). Samuel, a boy, is dressed for service like a priest while Eli's sons, real priests, behave like thieves.

a: a small robe
p: Samuel's robe, a gift from his mother, comes back at two key moments later in the book.
b: The me'il was an outer robe worn by people of standing. Hannah's yearly robe shows her love and her vow kept. The same garment returns twice: when Saul grabs it and it tears, Samuel says the kingdom has been torn from him (15:27–28), and at Endor the medium recognizes Samuel's ghost by his robe (28:14). Readers since the rabbis have followed this thread from a mother's gift to a prophet's sign.

a: took note of
p: The verb is the one used when "the LORD took note of Sarah" (Genesis 21:1).
b: Paqad means to visit, attend to or take note of. It is used when God acts to give a child or to rescue: "The LORD took note of Sarah as he had said" (Genesis 21:1), and when he takes note of his people in Egypt (Exodus 4:31). The narrator alternates short reports of Samuel growing (2:21, 2:26; 3:19) with the corruption of Eli's house, so the reader watches one family rise as another falls.

a: God can judge between them
p: Elohim can mean God or, in some legal texts, the judges acting for God.
b: The verb pillel means to arbitrate or step in as judge, and the related hitpallel means to pray, that is, to plead with the judge. Eli's point: in a quarrel between people, a third party can settle it; but when the LORD is the injured party, who is left to plead? Some translators read elohim here as "the judges" (compare Exodus 22:8–9), but the contrast with "the LORD" in the next line favors "God."

a: because the LORD meant to put them to death
t: Did God stop them from listening?
p: The text says they did not listen because the LORD wanted them dead. Readers have long asked what that means.
b: Like the hardening of Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 9:12), the line puts God's will behind human refusal. Jewish interpreters such as Maimonides taught that a sinner can sin so gravely that God withholds the chance to repent as part of the punishment, and they cited Pharaoh (Mishneh Torah, Repentance 6:3). Calvin read it as God's just judgment working through their own free and wicked choice. Many modern scholars see the narrator explaining a known outcome, the death of Hophni and Phinehas, as God's decision. The text does not say God made them sin.

a: kept growing up and doing well
p: Luke describes the boy Jesus in words that echo this verse.
b: Luke says that Jesus "kept moving forward in wisdom and in maturity, and in favor with God and with people" (Luke 2:52), and that the boy John "grew" (Luke 1:80). The pattern of Samuel, the child given to God who serves in the sanctuary and grows in favor, is one of several that Luke uses in his birth stories, along with Hannah's song. The Hebrew here is simple: the boy "kept going on, and growing, and good," with the LORD and with people.

a: a man of God
p: "Man of God" is an older title for a prophet. This one is never named.
b: Moses is called "the man of God" (Deuteronomy 33:1), and so are Elijah, Elisha and many unnamed prophets (Judges 13:6; 1 Kings 13:1). Samuel himself is called a man of God in 9:6. The message has two parts: the LORD chose Eli's ancestors in Egypt (2:27–28), and Eli's house will fall (2:30–36). The speech uses many words and ideas of Deuteronomy and the books that follow it, and most critical scholars see the hand of the Deuteronomistic editors, looking ahead to Solomon's time (1 Kings 2:27).

a: your ancestor's family
p: The "father's house" chosen in Egypt is probably Aaron's or Levi's. Some think Shiloh's priests came from Moses.
b: Chronicles traces Eli's descendant Ahimelech to Aaron's son Ithamar (1 Chronicles 24:3), and Josephus says the same. The house "chosen in Egypt" would then be Aaron's, whom God named as Moses' spokesman there. Frank Moore Cross argued that Shiloh's priests may have claimed Moses himself as ancestor, while Jerusalem's Zadokite priests claimed Aaron, and that the rivalry of the two lines lies behind texts like this one. The book never names Eli's father.

a: kick at
p: The rare verb pictures a well-fed animal kicking. It ties into the chapter's words about fat and weight.
b: Ba'at, "kick," appears elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32:15, where Israel grew fat and kicked. Here the priests "fatten" themselves on the offerings, Eli turns out to be "heavy" (4:18), and God says he will honor those who honor him. In Hebrew "heavy" and "honor" come from the same root (see 2:30). The Greek reads the line differently, "Why have you looked on my incense and my sacrifice with a shameless eye?" (see the variant).

a: I will honor the ones who honor me
p: In Hebrew, "honor" is "weight" and "scorn" is "lightness." The book plays on this through chapter 6.
b: The verb "honor" (kibbed) comes from kaved, "heavy," and "count for little" (qalal) means to be light. Eli honors (literally "makes heavy") his sons above God (2:29); Eli himself is "old and heavy" when he falls (4:18); his grandson is named Ichabod, "no glory (weight)" (4:21); the LORD's hand is "heavy" on the Philistines (5:6, 5:11); and they are told to give him honor so that he will make his hand "lighter" (6:5). Robert Polzin and others have traced this thread. The saying itself became a proverb of faith.
orig: מְכַבְּדַי אֲכַבֵּד וּבֹזַי יֵקָלּוּ (mekhabbeday akhabbed uvozay yeqallu)

a: There will not be an old man in your house for all time
p: The scroll and the main Greek text lack the first half of the Hebrew verse, which repeats 2:31. The Plain follows them.
b: The Masoretic Text begins the verse: "and you will look at distress in my dwelling, in all the good he does for Israel," words so unclear that readers have taken "distress" (tsar) as "a rival" priest or as Eli's family watching the sanctuary from outside. 4QSam-a and Codex Vaticanus lack those words, and 4QSam-a also lacks the end of 2:31. Since 2:31b and 2:32b say nearly the same thing, many scholars, including McCarter, see the Hebrew as a combination of two forms of the line. See the variants on 2:31 and here.

a: One man of yours I will not cut off from my altar
p: The prophecy points ahead to the slaughter of Eli's descendants at Nob, where one priest, Abiathar, escapes.
b: In 22:17–20 Saul has the priests of Nob, Eli's descendants, killed; only Abiathar escapes to David. He serves David for years, but Solomon removes him from the priesthood and sends him home to Anathoth, and the narrator says this happened to fulfill the LORD's word about the house of Eli at Shiloh (1 Kings 2:26–27). The prophet Jeremiah later comes from the priests of Anathoth (Jeremiah 1:1), and some scholars think he was a descendant of Eli.

a: a faithful priest
p: Jewish and Christian readers have named Samuel, Zadok or Christ as the priest God promises to raise up.
b: Kohen ne'eman, "a faithful priest," with "a house that stays faithful" (bayit ne'eman). Most readers, ancient and modern, see Zadok, who replaced Abiathar under Solomon (1 Kings 2:35) and whose line served in Jerusalem for centuries (Ezekiel 44:15). Some readers, Jewish and Christian, have suggested Samuel, who is called "trustworthy" (ne'eman) as a prophet in 3:20, but Samuel had no lasting priestly house. Many Christian readers have also seen Christ, whom Hebrews calls a "merciful and faithful high priest" (Hebrews 2:17). "My anointed one" here means the king (see 2:10).

a: the LORD's people passing around
p: The Hebrew can mean the people are spreading the report, or that Eli's sons are making the LORD's people sin.
b: Ma'avirim 'am-YHWH uses the verb 'avar, "pass." The Plain takes it as the people passing the report around, as many modern versions do. The King James Version and many commentators read it as "you make the LORD's people transgress": by abusing the sacrifices, the priests lead worshipers into sin. The Hebrew allows both, and the second fits Eli's next words about sinning against the LORD (2:25).

a: The LORD's word was rare in those days
p: The chapter opens with God silent and ends with God's word going out through Samuel to all Israel.
b: "Rare" (yaqar) also means "precious," as of jewels. The note sets the scene: in the time of the judges there were few prophets (only the prophetess Deborah and an unnamed prophet are mentioned, Judges 4:4; 6:8), and visions did not "break out" (nifrats), that is, they were not common. By the end of the chapter the LORD is "showing himself at Shiloh" again (3:21), and in 4:1 Samuel's word reaches all Israel. Amos 8:11 later speaks of a famine "of hearing the words of the LORD."

a: His eyes had started to go dim
p: Eli's failing eyes are a fact of old age, and also a picture of a priesthood that no longer sees what God is doing.
b: Like Isaac, whose dim eyes led him to bless the wrong son (Genesis 27:1), Eli cannot see well. He does not see what his sons are doing, he mistakes Hannah's prayer for drunkenness (1:13), and he needs three calls before he understands that the LORD is speaking (3:8). By 4:15 he is fully blind. Literary readers see a pattern; traditional readers add that Eli, for all his faults, recognizes God's voice in the end and accepts God's judgment humbly (3:18).

a: God's lamp was not yet out
p: The sanctuary lamp burned through the night, so this is the hour before dawn. It also hints at Israel's dim light.
b: The law told the priests to keep the lampstand burning "from evening to morning" (Exodus 27:20–21; Leviticus 24:2–4). So the call comes in the last hours of the night. Many readers also see a picture: the light of God in Israel was low, but not out. The same image is used of David's line, a "lamp" God keeps burning in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36; 2 Samuel 21:17).

a: Samuel lay in the LORD's temple
p: Sleeping in the sanctuary near the ark troubled later Jewish readers, who placed him in a side room.
b: Read simply, the boy slept in the shrine, near the ark. Later Jewish law allowed no one to sit or lie in the temple court except kings of David's line, so the Talmud explained that Samuel lay in the court of the Levites, and that the words "in the LORD's temple" belong with the lamp, which was burning there (Bavli Kiddushin 78b). In the wider ancient world people sometimes slept in a temple to receive a dream from a god, and some scholars compare that practice, called incubation. Here, though, Samuel is not seeking anything: the call comes unasked.

a: Here I am
p: Samuel's answer, hineni, is the answer of Abraham, Moses and Isaiah when God calls.
b: Hinneni means "here I am" or "I'm ready." Abraham says it when God calls him to sacrifice Isaac (Genesis 22:1), Jacob when God speaks at night (Genesis 46:2), Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:4), and Isaiah offers himself with "Here I am. Send me" (Isaiah 6:8). Three times he runs to Eli with "Here I am"; the fourth time, he answers the LORD with "Speak." The repetition gently shows that readiness alone is not enough: one must know whose voice is calling.

a: Samuel had not come to know the LORD yet
p: This is not unbelief. In Hebrew, "know" can mean personal experience, and Samuel had not yet heard God speak.
b: The verse explains why Samuel kept running to Eli: no word of the LORD had yet been "shown" (literally "uncovered") to him. The same words, "did not know the LORD," were used of Eli's sons (2:12), but the contrast is sharp: they would not, he had not yet. Rabbinic and Christian readers alike have used the verse to teach that faithful service can come before a personal word from God.

a: Your servant is listening
p: Hebrew eved means servant or slave. Calling oneself "your servant" is the polite way to address a superior or God.
b: 'Eved covers everything from a household slave to a royal official to a worshiper of God. The Plain translates it "servant" or "slave" by context: Samuel's "your servant" is humble speech, while the king's "slaves" in 8:16–17 are forced labor. Eli tells Samuel to say "Speak, LORD," but in 3:10 Samuel says only "Speak," without the name. Some rabbis took this as reverence; others simply as a boy's nervousness. The prayer "Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening" has become a classic of Jewish and Christian devotion.

a: the LORD came and took his stand there
p: The LORD "came" and "stood." The text later calls it a vision (3:15). Readers differ on what Samuel saw.
b: The verb yatsav, "take one's stand," suggests a presence, as when the LORD "stood" above the ladder in Jacob's dream (Genesis 28:13). Samuel's experience is called a mar'ah, "vision," in 3:15. The Targum softens it: "the LORD revealed himself." Many Christian interpreters took such appearances as visits of the Son before his birth; most Jewish interpreters understood a vision or voice rather than a body. The narrator stresses hearing more than seeing.

a: both their ears will ring
p: The same unusual phrase is used later of the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 21:12; Jeremiah 19:3).
b: The verb tsalal means to tingle or ring, as a bell does. Only here and in two prophecies of Jerusalem's fall is it used of the ears: in 2 Kings 21:12, for the evil of Manasseh, and in Jeremiah 19:3, at the Valley of Hinnom. The echo is deliberate on most readings: the end of Shiloh is a pattern for the end of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah himself makes the comparison (Jeremiah 7:12–14).

a: no sacrifice or grain offering will ever make atonement
p: Sacrifice could atone for sins done by mistake, but not for deliberate contempt. That is the point here.
b: Kipper, "make atonement," is the word for the cleansing that sacrifices bring. The law offered atonement for sins done unknowingly (Leviticus 4), but the one who sins "with a high hand," in open defiance, is cut off (Numbers 15:30–31). The priests who should have offered atonement for others have despised the very offerings that atone (2:17). The rabbis read the verse narrowly: sacrifices cannot atone for Eli's house, but Torah study and acts of kindness can (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18a).

a: He is the LORD. Let him do whatever looks good to him.
p: Is Eli humble or resigned? Readers disagree.
b: Many traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, admire Eli here: he accepts a terrible judgment without argument, like Aaron who "was silent" when his sons died (Leviticus 10:3). Others note that he does not repent, pray for his house or remove his sons, and read his words as passive resignation. The text gives no verdict. It does show that Eli insisted on hearing all of God's word, even against himself (3:17).

a: proven trustworthy
p: The word ne'eman, "faithful, trustworthy, firm," links Samuel to the "faithful priest" of 2:35.
b: Ne'eman means firm, reliable, faithful. God promised a "faithful priest" and a house that "stays faithful" (2:35); now Samuel is shown to be faithful as a prophet. The same word is used of Moses, "In all my house he is faithful" (Numbers 12:7), and of David's house (2 Samuel 7:16). The sign of a true prophet was that his words came true (Deuteronomy 18:22), as 3:19 says.

a: made himself known to Samuel by the word of the LORD
p: The LORD now reveals himself chiefly by his word. Readers note the move from sacrifice to prophecy at Shiloh.
b: Shiloh began as the place of the ark and the sacrifices; now it is the place where the LORD's word comes to a prophet. Many readers see here a turning point in Israel's history: from this point the prophets, not the priests, lead Israel's relationship with God. Jewish tradition counts Samuel as the first of the prophets after Moses, and Acts 3:24 speaks of "all the prophets from Samuel on." The Greek adds that Samuel was trusted as a prophet across the land and that Eli's sons went on in their evil way (see the variant here).

a: So what Samuel said reached all Israel
p: The first sentence of 4:1 finishes chapter 3. The Greek adds a sentence that explains why the war began.
b: Chapter divisions were added in the Middle Ages. This sentence belongs with 3:19–21: Samuel's word now reaches all Israel. Then the scene changes to war. Samuel disappears from the story until chapter 7, and the ark takes center stage. The Hebrew does not say who started the war; the Greek says the Philistines gathered against Israel (see the variant). Many critical scholars think the ark chapters were once a separate "ark story": Leonhard Rost marked it as 4:1b–7:1 with 2 Samuel 6, while Patrick Miller and J. J. M. Roberts argued that it began with Eli's sons in chapter 2 and ended at 7:1.

a: Ebenezer
p: Aphek guarded the coast road at the springs of the Yarkon. Ebenezer may be the village at Izbet Sartah, close by.
b: Aphek is Tel Aphek (Ras el-Ain), on the edge of the coastal plain, the Philistines' natural staging ground (29:1). Ebenezer, "stone of help," is not named until Samuel sets up the stone in 7:12, so the narrator uses the later name. Israeli archaeologist Moshe Kochavi suggested that Ebenezer is the small hilltop village of Izbet Sartah, about two miles east of Aphek, where one of the oldest alphabet inscriptions, a practice abecedary, was found. The identification is plausible but not certain.

a: about four thousand men
p: The Hebrew word for "thousand" can also mean a clan unit. That may matter for the large numbers here.
b: Elef means "thousand," but also a clan or a military unit raised from it (Judges 6:15; 10:19). George Mendenhall and others argued that many large army figures in early Israel counted units, not single men: "four elef" might be four units, much fewer than four thousand men. The idea is debated. The Plain gives the ordinary meaning and notes the other here.

a: Let it come into our camp and rescue us
p: Israel carries the ark into battle as if it would force God to fight. The story shows that God cannot be used that way.
b: The ark had led Israel in the wilderness and at Jericho, and Moses' cry when it set out was "Rise up, LORD! Let your enemies scatter" (Numbers 10:35). So the elders' plan has a basis. But they ask no prophet and no priest whether God wants this, and their words treat the ark as a weapon: "let it come ... and rescue us." The result is the worst defeat yet. Jeremiah warned his own generation with the same lesson: trusting in "the temple of the LORD" will not save a people who do not obey (Jeremiah 7:4, 12). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have drawn this lesson from the chapter.

a: who sits on the cherubim as his throne
p: The ark was pictured as the footstool of God's invisible throne, flanked by two cherubim.
b: The title "the LORD of Armies who sits on the cherubim" is linked to the ark (2 Samuel 6:2; Psalm 80:1; Psalm 99:1). Over the ark's cover stood two golden cherubim with wings spread (Exodus 25:18–22). Ancient Near Eastern kings sat on thrones whose sides were winged creatures, as on the carved sarcophagus of Ahiram of Byblos and on ivories from Megiddo. Israel's throne was empty: God was present but not shown. Chronicles calls the ark "the footstool of our God" (1 Chronicles 28:2).
r: Exodus 25:18–22; 2 Samuel 6:2; Psalm 80:1; Psalm 99:1; 2 Kings 19:15; 1 Chronicles 28:2

a: the Hebrews' camp
p: In 1 Samuel the name "Hebrews" is mostly used by foreigners, especially the Philistines, about Israelites.
b: 'Ivri, "Hebrew," is what Egyptians call Joseph and the Israelite slaves (Genesis 39:14; Exodus 2:6), and what the Philistines call Israel (4:9; 13:19; 14:11; 29:3). Israelites rarely call themselves that. Many scholars have compared the 'apiru or habiru of Late Bronze Age texts, including the Amarna letters, who were outsiders, soldiers for hire or rebels; the names may be related, though 'apiru was a social class, not a people.

a: struck Egypt down with plague after plague in the wilderness
p: The Philistines know the story of the plagues, but they get the place wrong and speak of many gods.
b: The plagues struck Egypt in Egypt, not "in the wilderness." The Philistines also speak of "these mighty gods," in the plural. Many readers think the narrator lets them garble Israel's story on purpose: they fear the LORD, but they do not know him. Some scholars emend the text to "with every plague and with pestilence." The irony is that the plague story is about to repeat itself in their own towns (chapters 5–6), with "heavy" hearts and a God who "made sport" of his enemies (6:6).

a: God's ark was captured
p: The capture of the ark was remembered for centuries as one of Israel's worst disasters.
b: Psalm 78 looks back: God "left his dwelling at Shiloh," gave his strength to captivity, and its priests "fell by the sword," while its widows "did not weep" (Psalm 78:60–64), which fits the death of Phinehas and his wife. The battle probably took place in the eleventh century BC. Nothing in Samuel says Shiloh was destroyed, but later Shiloh has no ark and Eli's family serves at Nob (21:1; 22:11), and Jeremiah treats Shiloh's fall as known (Jeremiah 7:12).

a: A Benjaminite ran from the fighting
p: Torn clothes and earth on the head mark mourning. A runner with the same signs brings David news of Saul's death.
b: Aphek to Shiloh is about twenty miles of rising ground. The runner's torn clothes and dirt on his head are signs of grief (Joshua 7:6; 2 Samuel 13:19). At the other end of the book, a man runs from Saul's last battle to David: "His clothes were torn and he had earth on his head" (2 Samuel 1:2). The book is framed by two defeats reported by two runners. A Jewish tradition recorded by Rashi says the runner was Saul himself, a Benjaminite.

a: His eyes stared without moving
p: The Hebrew says his eyes "stood." The same phrase is used of the old prophet Ahijah.
b: 'Enav qamah, "his eyes stood," means they were fixed and blind, perhaps from cataracts. The phrase is used of the prophet Ahijah, who was also blind with age (1 Kings 14:4). Eli's blindness completes the picture begun in 3:2, where his eyes had begun to grow dim.

a: the man was old and heavy
p: Eli falls because he was "heavy" (kaved). The same root means "honor" and "glory."
b: Eli had honored (literally "made heavy") his sons above God and grown fat on the offerings (2:29); now his weight breaks his neck. In 4:21 his grandson is named Ichabod, "Where is the glory (kavod)?" See 2:30 on how the book plays with the root. Many readers find the detail more than physical. Others, more cautious, see only an old man's sad end.

a: For forty years he had judged Israel
p: Eli is listed like the judges before him. He is the second-to-last judge; Samuel is the last.
b: The formula "he judged Israel X years" closes the stories of the judges (Judges 12:7; 15:20; 16:31). Eli's forty years round off his story the same way, and Samuel will be the last to "judge" Israel (7:15). Forty is often a round number for a generation. The Greek says twenty years (see the variant).

a: Ichabod
p: Ichabod probably means "Where is the glory?" or "No glory." The ark's capture is described as glory going into exile.
b: I-khavod joins a word that means "where?" or "not" with kavod, "glory," the weighty presence of God (Exodus 40:34). The verb galah means "go into exile": the ark is the first exile in Israel's history, long before Assyria and Babylon. Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD leave the temple before Jerusalem falls (Ezekiel 10:18–19), and Psalm 78:61 says God let "his beauty fall into the foe's hand." The dying mother's words are the true end of Eli's house.
orig: אִי־כָבוֹד ... גָּלָה כָבוֹד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל (i-khavod ... galah khavod miYisra'el)

a: Ashdod
p: The ark visits three of the five Philistine cities. Four have been excavated; Gaza lies under the modern city.
b: The five Philistine cities were Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron (6:17), each under its own ruler. Excavations at Tel Ashdod, Ashkelon, Tel Miqne (Ekron) and Tell es-Safi (Gath) show a new culture arriving around 1175 BC, with Aegean-style pottery, hearths and loom weights, among other signs. At Ekron a royal inscription found in 1996 names the city and its ruler Ikausu (Achish) son of Padi, who built a temple there in the seventh century BC. Gaza's ancient mound lies under the modern city and has had only small soundings. These finds anchor the Philistines of Samuel in real places.

a: the house of Dagon
p: Dagon was an old god of Syria, most likely a grain or storm god, not a fish god. The Philistines adopted him.
b: Dagan was worshiped along the Euphrates and in Syria from the third millennium BC, and at Ugarit Baal is called "son of Dagan." His name is most often explained from dagan, "grain," though some connect it with a word for rain clouds and see a storm god. The idea that he was half fish (from dag, "fish") is found in medieval Jewish commentators such as Radak, and most scholars now reject it. Judges 16:23 shows a feast for Dagon at Gaza. Captured gods and sacred objects were often set in the victor's temple as trophies, so the Philistines are showing that Dagon has beaten the LORD. No temple of Dagon has been excavated; the Philistine temples found so far are at Tell Qasile and at Ekron, where the temple inscription names a goddess, PTGYH.

a: Dagon lay face down on the ground
t: Captured gods in the ancient world
p: Ancient armies carried off their enemies' gods. Here the captured God humbles the god of the captors.
b: Assyrian and Babylonian texts often tell of conquerors carrying off the statues of defeated peoples' gods, and of the gods' later return. A Babylonian text called the Marduk Prophecy has Marduk himself describe his years in foreign lands. Patrick Miller and J. J. M. Roberts showed that the ark story follows this pattern closely, but turns it around: the captured God is not defeated, and the god of the victors falls on his face before him, as a servant bows to a king. The verdict on the parallel is solid: the story uses a known pattern on purpose, to mock it.

a: Dagon's head and the palms of both his hands lay cut off
p: Cutting off the head and hands was how ancient armies counted and shamed the dead. Dagon is treated as a slain enemy.
b: Egyptian reliefs at Medinet Habu show scribes counting piles of hands cut from dead enemies, and the Bible tells of hands and heads cut off in war (17:51; 31:9; Judges 8:6). Dagon's image ends up like a defeated soldier on the doorsill of his own temple. The irony is heavy: the Philistines will later hang Saul's head in Dagon's temple (1 Chronicles 10:10), and David will cut off Goliath's head (17:51).

a: do not walk on Dagon's doorsill
p: The verse explains a custom: Dagon's priests did not step on the doorsill. Zephaniah condemns a similar practice.
b: Thresholds were thought to be holy or risky places in many ancient cultures. Zephaniah condemns those "who leap over the threshold" (Zephaniah 1:9), which may be the same custom. The Greek adds here "but they leap over it." The phrase "down to this day" shows that the custom was still known in the writer's time. The Maccabean leader Jonathan burned the temple of Dagon at Ashdod about 147 BC (1 Maccabees 10:84).

a: swellings
p: The disease is uncertain. The Hebrew text writes one word and the reading tradition says a politer one.
b: The written Hebrew has 'ofalim, "swellings" or "mounds"; the scribes' reading tradition replaces it with techorim, a word that most rabbis took to mean hemorrhoids (Bavli Megillah 25b lists it among words read in a more decent form). Because mice come into the story (6:4–5), many modern scholars think of bubonic plague, whose swollen lymph nodes are "buboes," though plague carried by rats is not certainly known this early. Others suggest dysentery. The Plain uses "swellings," which fits both the written word and the sense.

a: all the Philistine rulers
p: The Philistines' leaders have a title, seren, found only for them. It may be a foreign word.
b: Seren, plural seranim, is used only for the five Philistine rulers (Joshua 13:3; Judges 3:3). Many scholars link it to the Greek tyrannos, "tyrant," or to a Luwian word, Luwian being a language of southern Anatolia. Either would fit a people who came from the Aegean world. In this chapter the rulers meet as a council, which suggests a league of city-states rather than one king.

a: God's hand weighed down very hard there
p: "The hand of the LORD" is heavy on the Philistines throughout the ark story, as it was on Egypt.
b: The phrase "the hand of the LORD" or "his hand" recurs through chapters 4–7 (4:8; 5:6, 7, 9, 11; 6:3, 5, 9; 7:13). In Exodus the LORD's hand brings the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 9:3). The verb "weigh down" is kaved, heavy (see 2:30). Miller and Roberts named their study of these chapters after the phrase. The Philistines' only hope is to make the hand lighter (6:5).

a: fortune-tellers
p: Isaiah 2:6 also links the Philistines with fortune-tellers. Here they give sound advice.
b: Qosemim are people who read signs to learn the will of the gods, a practice the law forbids to Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10). Isaiah 2:6 complains that Israel is full of fortune-tellers "like the Philistines." Yet here the Philistine priests and diviners understand what Israel's elders did not: the ark is not a tool, its God must be honored, and the hardening of Pharaoh is a warning (6:6).

a: a guilt offering
p: The Philistines send a guilt offering, the payment made to set right an offense against a god.
b: In Leviticus the asham, "guilt offering," makes amends for harm done to holy things, with payment added (Leviticus 5:14–16). The Philistines' gold is that kind of payment. The verb "pay back" (heshiv) is used again and again: they return the ark and return a payment. Similar gifts to angry gods are known across the ancient world. The Philistines' theology is not Israel's, but the narrator lets it work.

a: five swellings made of gold and five mice made of gold
t: Golden mice and Apollo of the mice
p: Gold models of the affliction were a way to send it away. Greek myth also links mice and plague.
b: Models of a diseased part of the body, offered to a god in hope of healing, are well known from Greek healing shrines, though mostly from later times. In the first book of Homer's Iliad, the priest Chryses calls on Apollo "Smintheus," a title usually explained as "god of mice," and Apollo sends plague on the Greek army. Since the Philistines came from the Aegean world, some scholars see a shared tradition linking mice, plague and a wronged god. The parallel is suggestive but loose: there is no sign of borrowing in either direction.

a: Why make your hearts heavy
p: The priests warn against making the heart heavy, Exodus's word for Pharaoh's stubbornness.
b: The Exodus story uses kaved, "heavy," for Pharaoh's stubborn heart (Exodus 8:15; 9:34). The Philistine priests use the same word and the same verb Exodus uses for what God did to Egypt: he "made sport" of them. In Exodus 10:2 God speaks of telling your children "how I made sport of Egypt" (Exodus 10:2). The Philistines have learned the lesson of Egypt better than Israel did, and they let the ark go.

a: build one new cart
t: A new cart and unyoked cows
p: Holy tasks call for things never used for anything else. David will later move the ark on a new cart too.
b: The red heifer must be one on which "No yoke must ever have come" (Numbers 19:2), and the heifer for an unsolved murder must never have pulled a yoke (Deuteronomy 21:3). The Philistines, perhaps by instinct, choose what is pure and unused. When David moves the ark from Kiriath-jearim, he too uses a new cart, with deadly results (2 Samuel 6:3–7), because the law said Levites should carry it on poles (Numbers 4:15).

a: mooing as they walked
p: Nursing cows would turn back to their calves. These walked away, crying, which showed the hand of God.
b: The test is built so that nature points one way and only God can make the cows go the other. Unused to a yoke and separated from their calves, they should have balked or turned home. Instead they go straight down the one road, "mooing as they walked," lowing for their calves but not turning aside "right or left," a phrase Deuteronomy uses for faithful obedience (Deuteronomy 5:32). Readers have long admired the irony that cows obey God better than Israel's priests.

a: Beth-shemesh
p: A border town between Judah and the Philistines, in the Sorek Valley, assigned to the priests.
b: Beth-shemesh, "house of the sun," stood on the north edge of Judah where the Sorek Valley climbs from the plain, near Samson's country. It was one of the towns given to the priests, Aaron's descendants (Joshua 21:13–16), which may explain the Levites of 6:15. Excavations at Tel Beth-Shemesh show an Iron Age I village that, unusually, has almost no pig bones, while nearby Philistine sites have many, a possible sign of an ethnic border.

a: offered the cows up to the LORD as a burnt offering
p: Cows, a cart for firewood and a stone for an altar: the people of Beth-shemesh offer what they have.
b: Leviticus asks for a male animal for a burnt offering (Leviticus 1:3), and Deuteronomy for one central altar (Deuteronomy 12:13–14). Here cows are offered on a field stone. Traditional readers note that the law of the one altar applied only once the LORD had a settled place, and that Shiloh had just fallen. Many critical scholars see 6:15, where the Levites arrive after the cart is already broken up, as a later addition that brings the scene into line with the law; others take it as a flashback.

a: for looking into the LORD's ark
t: Why were the men struck down?
p: Looking at, or into, the holy ark was forbidden even to most Levites. Readers have asked what exactly the men did.
b: The Hebrew ra'u ba'aron can mean "looked at" or "looked into" the ark. The law warned that even Kohathite Levites "must not go in and look at the holy things, not even for an instant" (Numbers 4:20). The Talmud gives several readings, from gazing into it to treating it without respect (Bavli Sotah 35a). The Greek tells the story differently: "the sons of Jeconiah did not rejoice" with the others (see the variant). The deaths make the point of 6:20: the LORD is holy, and his presence is dangerous as well as good.
orig: כִּי רָאוּ בַּאֲרוֹן יְהוָה (ki ra'u ba'aron YHWH)

a: Who is able to stand in front of the LORD, this holy God?
t: Who can stand before the holy God?
p: The question echoes through the Bible: Psalm 24, Malachi and Revelation ask who can stand before God.
b: "Stand before" means to serve or to survive in someone's presence. Psalm 24:3 asks who may stand in the LORD's holy place and answers, the one with clean hands and a pure heart. Malachi 3:2 asks who can stand when he appears, and Revelation 6:17 asks who can stand in the great day of wrath. After Nadab and Abihu died, Moses quoted the LORD: "In those who come near me I will show myself holy" (Leviticus 10:3). The men of Beth-shemesh learn what the Philistines learned.

a: Kiriath-jearim
p: A hill town on the Judah-Benjamin border, once a Gibeonite town. The ark stayed there until David's day.
b: Kiriath-jearim, "town of the forests," was one of the four Gibeonite towns (Joshua 9:17) and is also called Baalah and Baale-judah (Joshua 15:9; 2 Samuel 6:2). It is usually located at Deir el-Azar near Abu Ghosh, west of Jerusalem, where recent excavations led by Israel Finkelstein and Thomas Römer have explored a large hilltop platform. The ark rested there until David brought it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:2–3; 1 Chronicles 13:5–6).

a: set apart his son Eleazar as holy
p: Eleazar is "set apart" to guard the ark. Was he a priest or a Levite? The text does not say.
b: Qiddeshu means "they made holy," set apart for sacred service. Abinadab and Eleazar are not called priests or Levites. Chronicles insists that only Levites should carry the ark (1 Chronicles 15:2), and many traditional readers assume the family were Levites. Critical scholars often see an older practice here, before the priesthood was limited to Levites. The name Eleazar matches that of Aaron's son, but no link is drawn.

a: Twenty years went by
t: How long was the ark at Kiriath-jearim?
p: The twenty years lead up to Samuel's call at Mizpah. The ark stayed on through Saul's reign until David moved it.
b: If the ark stayed at Kiriath-jearim until David brought it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6), it was there through all of Saul's reign, much longer than twenty years. So most readers take the twenty years as the time until Israel turned back to the LORD under Samuel. The ark is mentioned only once in Saul's story (14:18), and there the Greek reads "ephod." Chronicles says that in Saul's days "we did not seek it" (1 Chronicles 13:3).

a: longed and wept after the LORD
p: The verb is rare and uncertain. It may mean Israel lamented, or that it gathered and turned back to the LORD.
b: Nahah elsewhere means to wail or lament (Micah 2:4; Ezekiel 32:18). "Wailing after the LORD" may mean longing for him as for someone lost. The Greek reads "looked to the LORD" and some scholars emend to "turned to the LORD." The Plain gives the likely sense. The verse prepares for Samuel's call to return "with your whole heart" (7:3).

a: the foreign gods and the Ashtoreths
p: Baal was the Canaanite storm god, and Ashtoreth (Astarte) a goddess of love and war. The plurals mean local forms.
b: The pair "the Baals and the Ashtoreths" sums up Canaanite religion in Judges (Judges 2:13; 10:6). Astarte was worshiped across the Levant, and the Philistines later hang Saul's armor in her temple (31:10). Her Hebrew name is usually vocalized Ashtoret with the vowels of boshet, "shame," a scribal way of mocking her. Samuel's words echo Jacob's "Put away the foreign gods" (Genesis 35:2) and Joshua's at Shechem (Joshua 24:23).

a: They drew up water and poured it out
p: No law describes this rite. The Targum reads it as pouring out the heart in repentance.
b: Drawing water and pouring it out "before the LORD" appears only here. The Targum explains: "they poured out their heart in repentance like water before the LORD," taking it as an image of prayer (compare Lamentations 2:19; Psalm 62:8). Others see a real rite of cleansing or of self-humbling, perhaps like David pouring out water as an offering (2 Samuel 23:16). Jewish tradition later connected water-pouring with the Feast of Booths (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9). With fasting and confession it marks a day of national repentance.

a: Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah
p: Mizpah, "the lookout," was a meeting place of the tribes. Here Samuel takes up the role of judge.
b: Mizpah of Benjamin is usually placed at Tell en-Nasbeh, about eight miles north of Jerusalem. The tribes met there before the war on Benjamin (Judges 20:1), Saul is chosen there by lot (10:17), and after Jerusalem fell it became the seat of the governor Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:6). "Judged" here likely means both settling disputes and leading the nation, as the judges did. Samuel is the last of the judges and the first of the prophets (Acts 13:20).

a: a lamb still nursing
p: Samuel offers a burnt offering though he is not called a priest. Readers explain this in different ways.
b: A lamb could be offered after its eighth day (Leviticus 22:27). The more debated point is that Samuel, not a priest, sacrifices. Chronicles counts him a Levite (1 Chronicles 6:28), and Jewish tradition held that a prophet could authorize sacrifice outside the rules in a time of need (as Elijah did, 1 Kings 18:30–38). Critical scholars note that in early Israel heads of families and leaders often offered sacrifices (Judges 6:26; 13:19). The real point of the verse is prayer: Samuel cries out, and the LORD answers (Psalm 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1).
r: Leviticus 22:27; 1 Chronicles 6:28; 1 Kings 18:30–38; Judges 6:26; Psalm 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1

a: That day the LORD thundered over the Philistines
p: Hannah sang that the LORD "thunders at them from the sky" (2:10). Here it happens.
b: The battle at Mizpah reverses the battle at Aphek. There Israel brought the ark and lost; here Israel repents and prays, and the LORD himself fights with thunder. The line from Hannah's song comes true: "he thunders at them from the sky" (2:10). God's thunder routs enemies in other battles too (Joshua 10:11; 2 Samuel 22:14–15). The verb "threw into confusion" (hamam) is the one used at the Sea of Reeds (Exodus 14:24).

a: He called it Ebenezer
p: Ebenezer means "stone of help." The stone and its words entered Christian hymns.
b: Samuel names the stone Even ha'ezer, "the stone of the help," and explains: "Up to this point the LORD has helped us." The battle of 4:1 was fought at a place already called Ebenezer, so the name now marks the reversal of that defeat. Standing stones as memorials appear often (Genesis 28:18; Joshua 4:9; Joshua 24:26). Robert Robinson's hymn "Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing" (1758) made the word famous in English: "Here I raise my Ebenezer."

a: They did not come into Israel's land any more
p: The summary says the Philistines were subdued all Samuel's days, yet Philistine garrisons appear in 10:5 and 13:3.
b: Readers have long noticed the tension. Philistine posts stand in Israel's land in Saul's time (10:5; 13:3, 19–23), and Saul is anointed to rescue Israel from them (9:16). Traditional readers take 7:13 to mean that the Philistines made no major invasion during Samuel's active leadership, which ended when he grew old (8:1). Many critical scholars see an idealized Deuteronomistic summary that makes Samuel a model judge. Literary readers see a contrast: under a praying judge Israel was safe; under kings it will have to fight.

a: travel around to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah
p: Samuel's circuit covered a small area, all within a day's walk of his home at Ramah.
b: Bethel, Gilgal, Mizpah and Ramah all lie in the hills of Benjamin and southern Ephraim, a region about twenty miles across. That suggests Samuel's direct authority was regional, though the text says he judged "Israel." Each place had sacred history: Bethel with Jacob (Genesis 28:19), Gilgal with Joshua (Joshua 4:19–20), Mizpah with the tribal assembly (Judges 20:1). Ramah, his home, gets its own altar.

a: he made his sons judges
p: Samuel repeats Eli's failure: his sons take bribes, and their failure becomes the reason Israel asks for a king.
b: Judges had no dynasty. When the people offered Gideon a hereditary rule, he answered, "The LORD will rule over you" (Judges 8:23), though his son Abimelech tried to seize it (Judges 9). Samuel appoints his sons, and like Eli's sons they fail. Literary readers note that the book does not spare its heroes: Samuel, who judged Eli's house, cannot keep his own. The names are pious ones: Joel, "the LORD is God," and Abijah, "my father is the LORD." Beersheba is at the far south, away from Samuel's own circuit.

a: they took bribes and bent justice
p: Samuel's sons break the law of judges in Deuteronomy almost word for word.
b: Deuteronomy 16:19 tells judges: "Do not bend justice. Do not play favorites. Do not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise" (Deuteronomy 16:19). Samuel's sons do exactly what the law forbids, and "went off chasing profit," the word betsa', dishonest gain. Samuel himself will later ask the people to say whether he ever took a bribe (12:3).

a: like all the nations
t: Was asking for a king a sin?
p: God says the people have rejected him, yet Deuteronomy allows a king. Readers have argued over this ever since.
b: Deuteronomy foresees the people saying, "I will set a king over me, like all the nations around me" (Deuteronomy 17:14), and permits it under limits. Samuel's elders use almost the same words. So was the request wrong? In the Talmud, Rabbi Judah held that appointing a king was a commandment, while Rabbi Nehorai said this chapter speaks only because of the people's grumbling; another view says the elders asked rightly but the common people wrongly, "like all the nations" (Bavli Sanhedrin 20b). Many critical scholars since Wellhausen see two sources, one for and one against kingship, side by side in chapters 8–12. Many literary and traditional readers say the problem is the motive: Israel wants a king to replace God, not to serve him.

a: Me they have turned down
p: The deepest objection to kingship in the book: the LORD was already Israel's king.
b: Gideon refused a crown with the words "The LORD will rule over you" (Judges 8:23). The Song of the Sea ends "The LORD will reign" (Exodus 15:18), and Deuteronomy 33:5 says the LORD "became king in Jeshurun." Martin Buber built his study Kingship of God around this theme, arguing that early Israel was a direct rule of God, broken by the demand for a human king. God's reply here is surprising: he agrees, and he tells Samuel to give them one anyway. Hosea later says God gave Israel a king in his anger (Hosea 13:11).

a: Listen to the voice of the people
p: God tells Samuel to listen to the people's voice, while the people will not listen to Samuel's.
b: Shema' beqol, "listen to the voice," also means "obey." God says it to Samuel three times (8:7, 8:9, 8:22), and the people refuse to do it to Samuel (8:19). The irony is pointed: God yields to the people's voice while they reject the prophet's. The same verb runs through the book, from Samuel's "Your servant is listening" (3:10) to Samuel's rebuke of Saul, that listening is better than sacrifice (15:22). The Plain keeps the phrase each time.

a: the ways of the king
p: Mishpat can mean a right, a custom or a rule. Here it is what a king will claim, not what the law allows him.
b: Mishpat hammelekh could be "the king's rights," "the king's practice" or "the law of the king." What follows (8:11–17) is a description of what kings did, not a law God gives. The Talmud records a debate: Rav Judah, quoting Samuel (the Talmudic teacher), said that everything in the passage is allowed to a king, while Rav said it was spoken only to frighten them (Bavli Sanhedrin 20b). In 10:25 Samuel writes a different document, mishpat hammelukhah, "the rules of the kingdom," which most readers connect with the limits of Deuteronomy 17:14–20.

a: Here is how the king who rules you will act
t: A real picture of ancient kingship
p: The list matches the practices of Canaanite city kings known from the archives of Ugarit and Alalakh.
b: Isaac Mendelsohn showed in 1956 that the items in 8:11–17 match how kings ruled in the Canaanite city-states of the Late Bronze Age: men drafted for chariot corps, royal farms worked by conscripts, women taken for palace work, land given to officials, a tenth taken in tax. So the speech need not be written after Solomon, as many critics once assumed; it fits the kings Israel's neighbors knew. Still, many readers hear Solomon in it: forced labor (1 Kings 5:13; 1 Kings 12:4), chariots (1 Kings 10:26) and officials paid in land.

a: He will take a tenth
p: Israel already gave a tenth to the LORD for the Levites. The king will take another tenth for himself.
b: The tithe belonged to the LORD and supported the Levites and the poor (Numbers 18:21; Deuteronomy 14:28–29). Samuel warns that the king will take his own tenth of grain, grapes and flocks (8:15, 8:17). Ancient kings in Ugarit and elsewhere did collect such taxes. The speech moves from sons to daughters, fields, slaves and herds, and ends with the people themselves: "you will end up as his slaves" (8:17).

a: you will end up as his slaves
p: The God who brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt warns that a king could make them slaves again.
b: The LORD has just reminded Samuel that he brought Israel up from Egypt (8:8). Now the warning ends with Israel as a king's slaves, the condition the exodus ended. Deuteronomy warns that the king must not "send the people back to Egypt" (Deuteronomy 17:16). Under Solomon and Rehoboam the people complain of a heavy yoke (1 Kings 12:4), and the northern tribes break away. The irony is part of the book's argument.

a: the LORD will not answer you
p: In Judges, Israel cried out and God rescued them. Here he warns he will not answer a cry about the king they chose.
b: The pattern of Judges was: Israel sins, cries out, God sends a rescuer (Judges 3:9). Once God refused: "That is why I will rescue you no more" (Judges 10:13). Samuel warns of the same refusal. Literary readers note that the warning is not the last word: the book goes on to show God answering Israel through David. But it does show that what Israel chooses has consequences God will not simply undo.

a: fight our wars
t: A king to fight our wars
p: The people want a king to fight for them. Up to now the LORD had fought for Israel, as at Mizpah (7:10).
b: The last thing the people ask is a king who will "march out at our head and fight our wars." In the previous chapter the LORD fought for them with thunder while Samuel prayed (7:10). Later David will tell Goliath that the battle belongs to the LORD (17:47). And Saul, the king they get, will die in battle with his sons (31:1–6). The request carries an irony the readers can see.

a: There lived a Benjaminite man named Kish
p: Saul's story opens with the same words as Samuel's in 1:1. Two births of leadership are set side by side.
b: Both begin vayhi ish, "there was a man," followed by a family tree (1:1; 9:1), as does Samson's story (Judges 13:2). Saul is from Benjamin, the tribe nearly wiped out in Judges 20–21 and from the town of Gibeah, scene of the outrage of Judges 19. Readers who know Judges cannot hear "Benjamin" and "Gibeah" without remembering. Kish is a gibbor chayil, a man of strength and wealth, like Boaz (Ruth 2:1).

a: a fine young man
p: The Hebrew word tov can mean handsome or good. The book will ask whether Saul's looks matched his heart.
b: Bachur vatov means a choice young man, good or good-looking, and "no one was finer (tov) than he." His height, a head and shoulders above everyone, is stressed again in 10:23. When Samuel later admires David's tall brother Eliab, God says, "Do not look at his appearance or his height," for the LORD looks on the heart (16:7). Many readers see that line as a comment on Saul. Others note that 9:2 is not ironic: Saul really was impressive, and God really chose him.

a: she-donkeys
p: Saul goes looking for his father's donkeys and finds a kingdom. Donkeys were wealth and sometimes royal mounts.
b: She-donkeys were valuable for breeding and riding, a sign of a wealthy family. Leaders in Judges ride donkeys (Judges 10:4; 12:14), and kings ride mules or donkeys (1 Kings 1:33; Zechariah 9:9). The story is a folk-tale shape that readers have loved: the young man sent on a small errand who stumbles on his destiny. Jewish tradition praised Saul's concern for his father, who would worry more about him than about the animals (9:5).

a: a man of God in this town
t: The seer in the unnamed town
p: The town is unnamed, and Samuel's name is held back until 9:14. An older tale of a nameless seer may lie behind it.
b: The servant knows of "a man of God" whose words come true, but Saul has never heard of Samuel, though 3:20 said all Israel knew him. The town is unnamed, though the land of Zuph (9:5) recalls Samuel's family (1:1). Many critical scholars think the story was first told of a local seer and later joined to Samuel's. Traditional readers answer that a farm boy from Benjamin need not know a prophet's face or town. Literary readers enjoy the suspense: the reader knows who the seer is before Saul does.

a: no present we can bring the man of God
p: Visitors brought gifts to seers. Some prophets refused them, and others were condemned for prophesying for money.
b: Jeroboam's wife takes bread, cakes and honey to the prophet Ahijah (1 Kings 14:3), and the Aramean general Naaman offers Elisha silver and gold, which he refuses (2 Kings 5:15–16). Micah condemns prophets who "tell fortunes for money" (Micah 3:11). A quarter shekel (9:8) was a small sum, perhaps three grams of silver. The gift was a courtesy, a way of showing respect, not a fee for a service.

a: the one now called a prophet was called a seer back then
p: A later editor explains an old word. The note shows that the book was put together some time after the events.
b: Ro'eh, "seer," is from the verb "see"; navi, "prophet," probably means "one called" or "one who calls out." The note stands oddly before 9:11, where "seer" is first used, so many scholars think it began as a note in the margin. It tells us that by the editor's time the word "seer" sounded old-fashioned. Chronicles still speaks of "Samuel the seer" (1 Chronicles 29:29).

a: the high place
p: A bamah was a local shrine on a hilltop. Before the temple they were accepted; later kings tore them down.
b: Bamah, "high place," was an open-air shrine with an altar, often on a hill, with a hall for sacrificial meals (9:22). With Shiloh fallen and no central sanctuary, Samuel leads worship at one. Kings says that before the temple "the people kept offering sacrifices at the high places" (1 Kings 3:2), and Solomon himself did so at Gibeon. Later prophets and kings condemned high places as centers of mixed worship (2 Kings 23:8), following Deuteronomy's law of one chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:5).

a: had opened Samuel's ear
p: To "uncover someone's ear" is a Hebrew way to say "tell a secret."
b: The idiom galah ozen pictures pushing back the hair or headcloth to whisper. Jonathan uses it when he promises to tell David Saul's plans (20:2, 12–13), and David uses it of God's promise (2 Samuel 7:27). The LORD tells Samuel his plan a day ahead, so that Samuel will know the man when he sees him.

a: as ruler over my people Israel
p: God tells Samuel to anoint Saul nagid, "ruler," not melekh, "king." Scholars debate why.
b: Nagid means one who goes in front, a leader. God uses it for Saul here and in 10:1, and for David (13:14; 2 Samuel 5:2; 2 Samuel 7:8), while the people use melekh, "king." Some scholars, such as Albrecht Alt and Baruch Halpern, take nagid as "king-designate," the one named by God before he is made king by the people. Others see a deliberate choice: God gives Israel a leader under him, not a king "like all the nations." On this site nagid used of a leader God designates is "ruler," and melekh is "king"; in other settings nagid can mean an official, such as an "officer in charge" (Jeremiah 20:1).

a: for I have seen my people; their cry has come to me
p: The words echo God's call of Moses at the burning bush.
b: At the bush the LORD said: "I have seen, yes seen, the suffering of my people who are in Egypt. I have heard their outcry" (Exodus 3:7). The Greek reads "the affliction of my people" (see the variant). Saul is introduced as a new Moses or a new judge, sent to rescue Israel from oppression, and the people's demand for a king (chapter 8) is answered by God's own concern for their suffering. The verse holds both views of kingship together.

a: This one will rule my people
p: The verb usually means "hold back" or "restrain." It may hint that the king's job is to keep the people in check.
b: 'Atsar normally means to stop, shut up or hold back, as God "shut" a womb (Genesis 16:2) or the sky (Deuteronomy 11:17). Used of ruling, it is unusual, and translators render it "govern," "restrain" or "rule." Some see a hint of the king as the one who keeps order in a land where "everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). The same verb is used in the longer text of 10:1.

a: who is it that all Israel longs for
p: Samuel's question can mean "who is Israel's desire?" or "whose is all that Israel desires?"
b: Chemdat Yisra'el means "what Israel desires" or "the best of Israel."
