Samuel may mean that Israel's longing for a king points to Saul, or that the best things of Israel will belong to Saul's family. Either way, Saul hears it as a hint of greatness and protests (9:21). Christian readers have sometimes linked the phrase to "the desire of all nations" in the old translation of Haggai 2:7, but that verse speaks of the treasures of the nations, not of a person.

a: I'm only a Benjaminite
p: Saul answers as Gideon did: my tribe is small and my family is the least.
b: Gideon said to the angel, "Look, my clan is the poorest in Manasseh, and in my father's house I count for least" (Judges 6:15), and Moses asked, "Who am I?" (Exodus 3:11). Benjamin really was the smallest tribe after the civil war of Judges 20–21. Saul's modesty seems sincere here, and he will hide among the baggage in 10:22. Samuel later reminds him that he was once small in his own eyes (15:17).

a: the thigh and what came with it
p: Saul is served the thigh, a choice portion that the law gave to priests.
b: In Leviticus the right thigh of a peace offering belongs to the priest (Leviticus 7:32–34). Saul, not a priest, is given it at a sacred meal, a sign of honor and perhaps of his new standing. The phrase "and what came with it" (vehe'aleha) is odd; many scholars, following Abraham Geiger, read veha'alyah, "and the fat tail," a prized part of a sheep (Leviticus 3:9). The Hebrew does not name the speaker of "There, that is what was saved"; the Plain supplies Samuel, as most readers do.

a: the flask of oil
p: Pouring oil on the head marked a person for a special office. Egyptian pharaohs anointed their vassal kings too.
b: In Israel priests, kings and once a prophet were anointed (Exodus 29:7; 1 Kings 19:16). Samuel uses a small flask (pakh); for David he will use a horn (16:13). Outside Israel, an Amarna letter recalls that Pharaoh's grandfather "put oil on the head" of a Syrian vassal king to make him king (EA 51). Anointing set a person apart and showed whose servant he was. Samuel also kisses Saul, a sign of honor or homage (compare Psalm 2:12). From this rite comes the title "the LORD's anointed," in Hebrew meshiach YHWH (see 2:10).

a: Rachel's grave in Benjamin's territory
p: Genesis places Rachel's tomb near Bethlehem; this verse puts it on Benjamin's border, north of Jerusalem.
b: Genesis says "Rachel died, and they buried her on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem" (Genesis 35:19), and the traditional Rachel's Tomb stands just north of Bethlehem. But here the tomb lies on Benjamin's border, and Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping in Ramah, north of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18). Many scholars think the original tradition placed Ephrath in Benjamin, and that "which is Bethlehem" was a later note. Others think the route here passed near a southern site. Zelzah is otherwise unknown; the Greek reads it as "leaping greatly."

a: where the Philistines have a post
p: Philistine forces were stationed inside Israel's hill country. Jonathan will strike one in 13:3.
b: Netsiv can mean a garrison, a governor or a standing pillar marking control. Whichever it means, the Philistines held positions deep in Benjamin, which explains God's words in 9:16 and the war that begins in chapter 13. "Gibeah of God" may be Geba or Saul's own Gibeah. Samuel's instructions to Saul in 10:7, "do whatever the moment calls for," seem to point him toward this post.

a: a band of prophets
p: Groups who prophesied with music and strong emotion appear here and in Elisha's day. Mari had similar prophets.
b: These prophets come down from the shrine with harp, drum, flute and lyre, "prophesying," a verb that here means speaking or acting in an ecstatic state. Music could bring on prophecy (2 Kings 3:15). Later "sons of the prophets" lived in groups around Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2:3; 4:38). Letters from Mari on the Euphrates, from the eighteenth century BC, mention ecstatic prophets (muhhum) and "answerers" who gave messages from the gods. The Bible does not judge these bands; Samuel seems to lead them (19:20).

a: The Spirit of the LORD will sweep down on you
p: The verb is the one used for the Spirit coming on Samson. It is a sudden, powerful seizing.
b: Tsalach means to rush or break through. The Spirit of the LORD "swept down" on Samson before he tore apart a lion (Judges 14:6), and will sweep down on Saul again to rouse him to war (11:6) and on David at his anointing (16:13). The same verb is later used of "an evil spirit from God" on Saul (18:10). In the Hebrew Bible this kind of Spirit gives power for a task; it is not described as a permanent indwelling.
orig: וְצָלְחָה עָלֶיךָ רוּחַ יְהוָה (vetsalechah alekha ruach YHWH)

a: You are to wait seven days
p: This command will become Saul's first great failure, in chapter 13.
b: Samuel tells Saul to wait at Gilgal for seven days until he comes to offer sacrifices. In 13:8–14 Saul waits seven days, Samuel is late, the army begins to scatter, and Saul offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives as he finishes. Many readers see the command here as the first rule of Saul's kingship: the king must wait for the prophet's word. Critical scholars note that the command seems to skip over chapters 11–12 and connect directly with chapter 13.

a: God gave him another heart
p: Saul is "turned into another man" and given "another heart." Was this a conversion or an equipping for office?
b: In Hebrew the heart is the center of thought and will. God's change of Saul's heart prepares him to lead. Jewish interpreters generally saw it as wisdom and courage for kingship. Many Christian interpreters, such as Calvin, also took it as a gift for his office rather than a new birth, since Saul later turns from God. Others see a real spiritual change that Saul did not keep. Compare the promise of a "new heart" for all Israel in Ezekiel 36:26.

a: Is Saul among the prophets too?
p: The saying expressed surprise that someone acted out of character. The book gives it a second origin in 19:24.
b: The people are astonished to see the son of a landowner among the ecstatic prophets. The saying became a proverb for anyone found in an unexpected role. 19:24 gives another occasion for it, when Saul strips and lies prophesying before Samuel; many critics see two traditions about the proverb, while traditional readers see the second event as reviving the old saying. Whether the proverb praised Saul or mocked him is debated (see 10:12).

a: And who is their father?
p: A puzzling answer. It may mean that prophecy does not come by birth, so even Kish's son can prophesy.
b: Several readings are offered. Prophecy is not inherited, so it does not matter whose son Saul is; God gives it to whom he wills, which is roughly Radak's view. Or it scorns the prophets as men of no family, so Saul lowers himself by joining them. Or "father" is the title of a prophet band's leader (2 Kings 2:12; 6:21), and the man asks who leads them. The Greek, Syriac and Latin read "his father," pointing back to Kish (see the variant).

a: he went to the high place
t: To the high place, or home?
p: Saul's next scene is with his uncle, so some read "he went home" instead of "to the high place."
b: Habbamah, "to the high place," is what the Hebrew has. Because 10:14 has Saul talking with his uncle, perhaps at home, some scholars since Wellhausen have read habbaytah, "home." The Greek has "to the hill." The change is a guess, and the Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: he told him nothing
p: Saul does not tell his uncle about being anointed. Readers differ on whether this is modesty, caution or fear.
b: Many traditional readers praise Saul's humility: he does not boast of his anointing, and he hides at his public choosing (10:22). Others see prudence: talk of a new king in a land with Philistine posts could be dangerous. Literary readers note a pattern of Saul holding back, and some see the first sign of a man unready for the role. The uncle is unnamed; many readers think of Ner, father of Abner (14:50).

a: today you have turned down your God
t: Two or three stories of Saul's rise?
p: Saul becomes king three times: by secret anointing, by lot and by victory. Readers explain the sequence differently.
b: Saul is anointed privately (9:1–10:16), chosen publicly by lot at Mizpah (10:17–27), and acclaimed at Gilgal after his victory (11:1–15). Many critical scholars see separate accounts, some friendly to kingship and some hostile, woven together. Others, such as Baruch Halpern and V. Philips Long, see a known pattern of accession: designation by God, a deed that proves the man, then public confirmation. Samuel's speech here repeats God's verdict of 8:7. The people get what they asked for, and are told it is a rejection of God.

a: the lot fell on the tribe of Benjamin
p: The process of choosing Saul is the same one used to find Achan, the man who stole from Jericho.
b: In Joshua 7:14 the guilty man is found step by step: tribe by tribe, clan by clan, household by household, man by man, and the verb is nilkad, "taken." Saul is "taken" the same way. The method was a normal way to let God choose, but some literary readers, such as Robert Alter and Robert Polzin, think the echo is deliberate: the lot that found a guilty man now finds the king the people's sin demanded. The same method will later expose Jonathan (14:41–42).

a: he is hiding among the baggage
p: The future king is found hiding among the baggage. Humility, fear or both?
b: A rabbinic tradition praised Saul here as humble, unwilling to grasp at honor. Many modern readers see fear or a lack of confidence, the first hint of the man who will later be afraid of the Philistines (17:11) and of David (18:12). The LORD himself answers the people's question, which shows that he, not the people, is choosing. The tall man hidden among the bags is also a comic picture, and the narrator may intend that.

a: Long live the king!
p: The shout was the formal acclaiming of a new king, heard again at Solomon's and Joash's coronations.
b: Yechi hammelekh, "may the king live," is the cry of acclaim at Solomon's anointing (1 Kings 1:25, 34, 39) and at the crowning of the boy king Joash (2 Kings 11:12). It is the people's part in making a king. Here the chosen man is the one the people wanted, tall and impressive, and the LORD's choice agrees with the people's taste.

a: the rules of the kingdom
p: Samuel writes down the rules of the kingdom and lays the scroll before the LORD, as treaties were stored in temples.
b: This is the first written constitution for a king in the Bible. Its contents are not given, but most readers connect it with Deuteronomy's law of the king, who must "write for himself a copy of this law on a scroll" (Deuteronomy 17:18) and must not lift his heart above his brothers. Ancient treaties were placed in temples before the gods as witnesses, and the tablets of the covenant lay in the ark (Deuteronomy 10:5). Israel's king, unlike the kings of 8:11–17, was to be under a written law.

a: God had touched in their hearts
p: The Hebrew says "the army" or "the force" went with Saul. The Greek says "men of valor."
b: The Masoretic Text has hachayil, "the force" or "the army," while the Greek has "sons of power," that is, brave men, which many scholars prefer. Either way, Saul begins with a loyal core whose hearts God had moved, against the "worthless men" of 10:27. Gibeah becomes the capital of the first kingdom.
orig: הַחַיִל אֲשֶׁר־נָגַע אֱלֹהִים בְּלִבָּם (hachayil asher-naga' elohim belibbam)

a: brought him no gift
p: A gift to a king was a sign of loyalty. The refusers are "worthless men," like Eli's sons.
b: Bringing a minchah, a gift or tribute, to a new king was the way to accept his rule (1 Kings 10:25; 2 Samuel 8:2). The men who refuse are "sons of beliyya'al" (see 1:16), and their question, "How will this one rescue us?", sets up the next chapter, where he does exactly that. Saul's response, in the Masoretic Text, is silence; in the Dead Sea scroll and the Greek, the story moves straight on to Nahash (see the variant).

a: Nahash, king of the Ammonites, had been harshly oppressing the Gadites and the Reubenites
p: This paragraph, lost from the Masoretic Text, is found in the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a and was known to Josephus.
b: In 1952 scroll fragments of Samuel were found in Cave 4 at Qumran. The largest, 4QSam-a, copied about 50–25 BC, contains a paragraph before 11:1 that tells of Nahash's earlier campaign against the tribes east of the Jordan. Josephus, writing about AD 94, tells the same story (Antiquities 6.68–70), so his Bible had it. Frank Moore Cross argued that it is original and was lost when a scribe's eye skipped. Others, such as Alexander Rofé, think it is an early expansion. It explains why seven thousand refugees were in Jabesh, and why Nahash's threat in 11:2 was not empty. See the variant for the evidence.

a: Jabesh-gilead
p: Jabesh had old ties with Benjamin, and its people will repay Saul's rescue at his death.
b: Jabesh-gilead lay east of the Jordan, probably at Tell Abu al-Kharaz or Tell el-Maqlub by the Wadi Yabis. In Judges 21 the other tribes destroyed Jabesh for not joining the war against Benjamin, and gave its four hundred girls as wives to the Benjaminite survivors (Judges 21:8–14). Many Benjaminites, perhaps Saul's own family, would have had mothers from Jabesh. At the end of the book the men of Jabesh will walk all night to take down Saul's body from the wall of Beth-shan (31:11–13).

a: I put out every right eye you have
p: Josephus explains that a soldier covered his left eye with his shield, so losing the right made him useless in war.
b: Josephus says Nahash put out right eyes "so that, since their left eyes were covered by their shields, they might be wholly unfit for war" (Antiquities 6.70). Blinding was a known punishment for rebels and captives: the Philistines blinded Samson (Judges 16:21), and the Babylonians blinded King Zedekiah (2 Kings 25:7). Nahash's aim was also shame: "a disgrace laid on all Israel." The word for "disgrace" (cherpah) is used when Goliath taunts Israel (17:26).

a: following the oxen
p: The newly chosen king is still plowing when the call comes, like Gideon threshing and Elisha plowing.
b: Gideon was beating out wheat when the angel came (Judges 6:11), and Elisha was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah called him (1 Kings 19:19). Roman tradition tells of Cincinnatus, called from his plow to save Rome and returning to it afterward (Livy, History of Rome 3.26). The farmer-hero is a widespread folk theme, and there is no link of borrowing between these stories; the shared shape says that a true leader is called from ordinary work, not from seeking power.

a: hacked them into pieces
p: Saul's summons recalls the Levite who cut up his concubine and sent her body through Israel in Judges 19.
b: In Judges 19:29 a Levite of Ephraim "cut her up, bone by bone, into twelve pieces. Then he sent her to every corner of Israel" (Judges 19:29), and all Israel gathered "like one man" to punish Gibeah (Judges 20:1). Now a man of Gibeah sends pieces of oxen to call Israel to rescue Jabesh, the town once destroyed in that war. Most readers see a deliberate reversal. A letter from Mari tells of an officer who proposed killing a prisoner and sending his head around the towns so that the troops would assemble quickly, a similar use of fear.

a: Bezek
p: Bezek lay west of the Jordan, opposite Jabesh. The count names Judah separately from Israel.
b: Bezek is usually placed at Khirbet Ibziq, about a day's march across the Jordan from Jabesh. The count lists "Israelites" and "men of Judah" separately, as Samuel often does (15:4; 17:52; 2 Samuel 2:4). Some critics see the later split between the northern kingdom and Judah in this way of speaking; others see an older division between Judah and the northern tribes. On the size of the numbers, see 4:2 and the variant.

a: you can do to us anything you think is good
p: The men of Jabesh tell Nahash what he wants to hear, using words that also hide a trap.
b: "Tomorrow we will come out to you" sounds like surrender to Nahash; to the reader it means they will come out to fight with Saul's army. "Do to us whatever is good in your eyes" echoes the phrase of Judges, "everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes," and Eli's "let him do whatever looks good to him" (3:18). The trick works.

a: In the morning watch
t: A dawn attack in three groups
p: Saul splits his army into three, as Gideon did, and attacks before dawn.
b: The night was divided into watches; the morning watch was the last, before sunrise (Exodus 14:24). Dividing the army into three companies was a common tactic in Judges: Gideon (Judges 7:16) and Abimelech (Judges 9:43) used it. Saul acts like one of the judges: the Spirit comes on him, he musters the tribes, and he wins a rescue. His first act as king looks like a judge's act.

a: today the LORD has won a rescue in Israel
p: Saul refuses to execute those who had despised him, and gives the LORD the credit.
b: The people want to kill the men of 10:27. Saul says no, because this is a day of the LORD's rescue (teshu'ah). Many readers see Saul at his best: generous, humble, giving God the glory. David will show the same mercy to his opponents on the day of his victory (2 Samuel 19:22). The contrast with Saul's later violence against Jonathan (14:44) and the priests of Nob (22:17–19) is part of the tragedy of his story.

a: make the kingdom new
p: "Make new" suggests the kingdom already existed after 10:24. It may mean to confirm it, after the doubters of 10:27.
b: Chiddesh means "make new" or "renew." Saul had already been acclaimed at Mizpah (10:24), so many readers take this as confirming his rule now that he has proved himself and silenced the doubters. Many critics think Samuel's "renew" is an editor's join between two stories that once each told how Saul became king. Gilgal, where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 4:19–20), is a fitting place for a new beginning.

a: they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD
p: Peace offerings were shared meals of joy. Chapter 12, Samuel's farewell, takes place at this gathering.
b: Shelamim, "peace offerings," were sacrifices eaten by the worshipers in a festive meal with God. Covenant renewals often ended with such meals (Exodus 24:5, 11; Deuteronomy 27:7). The great joy of Saul and all Israel is the high point of his reign. Samuel's speech in chapter 12 is given at this same assembly.
